realism_constraints: No modern forensic DNA analysis available
Telephones and automobiles exist but are limited in use
Scientific instruments like microscopes and early polygraphs can be used
location: New York City, including Norwood and Jarvis residences and Atlantic City
institution: New York Police Department, Inspector Druet's Homicide Bureau

cast.public_persona: greatest living master of scientific criminal investigation

cast.name: Calvin Norwood

cast.public_persona: host and collector of crime relics
cast.private_secret: knows more about the wallet and letters than he admits

cast.name: Oliver Jarvis
cast.private_secret: financial troubles and quarrel with wife

cast.name: Victor Marchal

surface_summary: Mrs. Evelyn Jarvis is found strangled in a crime museum, her body brought there mysteriously. The investigation reveals blackmail involving mysterious letters and a missing wallet tied to a decade-old murder, with suspicion falling on various acquaintances.
accepted_facts: Evelyn Jarvis was murdered and found in Norwood's crime museum
She was being blackmailed with letters made of macaroni paste
A wallet containing letters related to a ten-year-old murder disappeared from the museum
Victor Marchal, the blind secretary, died by apparent suicide but left a signed confession
inferred_conclusions: Captain Marchal was the murderer driven by unrequited love
Oliver Jarvis killed his wife out of financial desperation
The murder occurred in Evelyn's own home
mechanism_description: Leonidas Hoyos, presumed dead for ten years, was the blackmailer who threatened Evelyn Jarvis. He killed her in the Norwood museum when she came to retrieve incriminating letters he had hidden. Victor Marchal overheard the crime and was murdered by Hoyos to silence him, but left a hidden signed statement that led to Hoyos' identification and capture.
delivery_path: Hoyos lured Evelyn to the museum where he was hiding
A struggle ensued and Hoyos strangled Evelyn
Victor Marchal overheard the murder and wrote a secret confession
Hoyos killed Marchal to prevent exposure
Marchal's confession was hidden in the typewriter drawer
McCarty decoded the confession using a microscope
The group confronted Hoyos leading to his capture
outcome_result: Leonidas Hoyos is identified as the murderer and brought to justice.

false_assumption.statement: Captain Marchal killed Evelyn Jarvis out of jealous passion.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Marchal's nervous behavior and physiological reactions during Terhune's experiment suggested guilt. His close presence at the crime scene and emotional turmoil supported this view.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It obscures the true culprit, Hoyos, who manipulated the situation and killed Marchal to silence him. Marchal was a victim, not the perpetrator.

supporting_points: His presence in the museum at the time of murder
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Ignored evidence of Hoyos' presence and Marchal's protective actions; failed to account for the staged suicide and missing bullet.

red_herrings.description: Oliver Jarvis' financial losses and inconsistent alibi suggested motive and opportunity.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: His financial troubles were real but unrelated to the murder; he was grieving and not involved.

red_herrings.description: Margot's insistence that the dressing-room was undisturbed and her suspicious behavior raised doubts.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Margot was loyal and truthful; the dressing-room was ransacked after her last visit.

closed_circle.rationale: All had access to the museum and motive or opportunity, but only Hoyos had the secret past connection and means to commit the murder.

time_anchors: letters sold to Norwood three days before murder
wallet last seen at 3 pm Friday
time_windows: Oliver Jarvis' unexplained absence between 3 and 6 pm
Marchal alone in house afternoon of murder
access_actors: Oliver Jarvis (keys to house and museum)
access_objects: Norwood house and Jarvis house back yards

inference_path.observation: The museum door had fine scratches around the keyhole
inference_path.correction: The door was opened with a spider lockpick
inference_path.effect: Indicates forced entry by someone with lockpicking skill
required_evidence: Close-up photograph of scratches around museum door keyhole
Witness statement of Victor Marchal about museum door being locked

inference_path.observation: A single glove was found wedged on the ladder to the museum window
inference_path.correction: The glove belonged to the murderer who wore gloves to avoid fingerprints
inference_path.effect: Identifies presence of intruder climbing ladder
required_evidence: Physical glove with oil and grease stains found on ladder
Inventory of Oliver Jarvis' motoring gloves including matching pair

inference_path.observation: Evelyn's dressing-room was ransacked but Margot claimed it was undisturbed at 8 pm
inference_path.correction: The ransacking occurred after Margot's last visit, possibly by Oliver Jarvis' brother
inference_path.effect: Suggests staging and attempts to mislead investigators
required_evidence: Margot's testimony about dressing-room condition at 8 pm
Etta Barney's confession about letting in her brother Dick

inference_path.observation: Victor Marchal wrote a signed statement but the typewriter ribbon was broken
inference_path.correction: The statement was invisible to the naked eye but detectable by microscope
inference_path.effect: Provides direct evidence implicating the murderer
required_evidence: Signed paper with indentations from typewriter keys
Microscopic analysis of paper showing hidden text

inference_path.observation: Two shots were fired from Marchal's pistol but only one bullet entered the body
inference_path.correction: The second shot was a blank fired to simulate suicide
inference_path.effect: Shows murder was staged to look like suicide
required_evidence: Ballistics report on pistol and cartridge shells
Position of furniture and powder marks in library

inference_path.observation: The blackmail letters were made of macaroni paste and referenced the 26th of each month
inference_path.correction: The 26th refers to the date of the original murder of Hoyos
inference_path.effect: Connects blackmail to past crime and Hoyos' identity
required_evidence: Macaroni paste letters found in Mrs. Jarvis' possession
Coroner's inquest records of Hoyos' death on 26th May

inference_path.observation: Kate Stricker sold the letters to Norwood but denies knowledge of murder
inference_path.correction: She was innocent but aware of the letters' significance
inference_path.effect: Exonerates Kate and focuses suspicion on Hoyos
required_evidence: Billings' butler statement about Kate's visit

discriminating_test.design: McCarty arranged a gathering of all key persons at his rooms, including police and witnesses, to confront the murderer with the evidence and provoke a reaction. The test relied on psychological pressure and the presence of incriminating items to elicit confession or reveal guilt.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The test revealed the identity of the murderer as Leonidas Hoyos by his reaction and the corroboration of Victor Marchal's signed confession.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The murderer reveals himself by involuntary behavior or confession under the pressure of the assembled evidence and witnesses.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given all essential clues including the blackmail letters, the missing wallet, the glove on the ladder, the broken typewriter ribbon, and Victor Marchal's signed confession. The narrative provides detailed timelines, alibis, and character motives. The scientific experiment and physiological tests offer insight into suspects' reactions. The solution is logically deduced from these facts, allowing an attentive reader to solve the case.
